# Prepping Land for Your Manufactured Home: What You Need to Do Before Delivery Day


Published On: October 30, 2026


•


10 min read


•


> **Quick answer:** To put a manufactured home on private land, the parcel must meet three sets of rules: local zoning, federal HUD installation standards and your lender’s requirements. On private land, the landowner is usually responsible for site work, including grading, septic or sewer, utility connections and a driveway, unless your retailer agrees in writing to handle it. Check five things before you close on the land: zoning, flood zone, utilities and septic, legal access and HUD design zones.


Here’s a hypothetical scenario. A buyer finds a beautiful affordable lot with a great view and makes an offer. Then they learn the lot needs a soil test for septic. It sits partly in a flood zone. And it reaches the road only across a neighbor’s property, with no recorded easement. Well, now that perfect lot doesn’t look so perfect. But don’t worry – each of those issues is a question with an answer – if you ask before you buy.


Here’s everything you need to know (and do) to make sure your perfect plot of land is ready for your new Cavco[manufactured home](https://www.cavcohomes.com/find-a-floor-plan) .


Don’t have land yet? Here’s


[how to find land for a manufactured home](https://blog.cavcohomes.com/how-to-find-land-for-a-manufactured-home-a-complete-guide-links/) .


## **What rules decide whether a manufactured home can go on a lot?**


Local zoning, HUD’s installation standards and lender requirements all apply, and a parcel can pass one and fail another. The[HUD code](https://blog.cavcohomes.com/what-is-the-hud-code-for-manufactured-homes/) is the federal construction and safety standard every manufactured home in the U.S. must meet. A home built to it carries a HUD certification label and a data plate.


Rules differ by state and local jurisdiction, so each section below identifies who you need to contact. Every state either runs its own manufactured home installation program or falls under HUD’s, and both include licensing or approval of installers. Retailers typically coordinate delivery and installation. Either the retailer or its installing subcontractor must meet the installation rules that apply.


It’s always best to get the retailer’s installation responsibilities and warranty coverage in writing. Cavco homes are sold through[Cavco-owned stores](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-retailers) and independent[local retailers](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-retailers) . Your retailer can tell you which site preparation, delivery and installation services your quoted price includes.


## **What should you check before you buy land for a manufactured home?**


Run five checks in order. Each can stop a project before any dirt moves.


1.


### **Is a manufactured home allowed by zoning?**


Ask the local planning office, in writing, whether a HUD-code manufactured home is allowed by right or only with a special permit or hearing. Then get the minimum lot size, the setbacks, and any appearance, foundation, deed, or HOA rules. Some localities restrict manufactured housing, so ask before you buy. A permit application may require a site plan showing setbacks, property markers, driveway grade, and water and sewer locations.


If local rules don’t allow HUD-code homes, ask about modular. A modular home follows state and local building codes instead of the HUD code.


1.


### **Is the land in a flood zone?**


Look up the parcel on FEMA’s flood map service, then ask the local floodplain administrator what applies. FEMA’s National Flood Insurance Program rules require manufactured homes in flood hazard areas to be elevated and anchored to a permanent foundation. Local ordinances set the exact height, usually measured from the base flood elevation, which is the flood height shown on the local map. Some ordinances add a safety margin, so no single national number applies.


Ask whether your foundation type needs flood openings, and ask your lender whether flood insurance is a loan condition. FEMA’s guide


[Protecting Manufactured Homes from Floods and Other Hazards (P-85)](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-08/fema_p85.pdf) covers the technical detail.


1.


### **Does the lot support septic and a well?**


Outside city limits, a manufactured home on private land will likely need a well and a septic system. Ask the local health department about well rules and water testing. Ask, too, whether your local government blocks new septic systems where public sewer is available.


Most communities require a professional site evaluation before issuing a septic permit. The evaluator checks soil, slope, depth to groundwater and bedrock, and required distances from wells and neighboring systems. Part of that work is usually a perc test, which measures how fast water drains through the soil. Poor soil can force a costlier engineered system or rule out the site.


You can make your land purchase contingent on a passing soil evaluation.


1.


### **Does the lot have legal access?**


Lenders look for a home on a publicly maintained street, or on a private road covered by an enforceable access and maintenance agreement. If your driveway crosses someone else’s land, you may need a recorded easement. A real estate attorney or title company can tell you what the document should say.


1.


### **Will the home match the parcel’s HUD design zones?**


Every manufactured home is built for a specific[wind zone](https://blog.cavcohomes.com/wind-zones-manufactured-homes/) , roof-load (snow) zone and thermal zone. The data plate lists the wind and roof-load zones, and the home’s heating and cooling certificate lists the thermal zone. Under HUD’s installation rules (24 CFR §3285.103), a home can’t be installed in a harsher zone than the one it was designed for. Check your parcel’s zones before you pick a floor plan. This matters most if you’re buying land in a different region from where you priced the home.


Then walk the lot. Look for steep slopes, standing water, trees and soft ground, and avoid any spot where water can pool.

## **What will a lender require for a manufactured home on land?**


Lender rules can shape the site as much as building code does. Real property means the home is legally part of the land, not titled like a vehicle. That status usually opens the door to a standard mortgage.


A home on leased land, or one never converted, is typically financed with a personal-property loan ([chattel loan](https://blog.cavcohomes.com/what-is-a-chattel-loan-manufactured-home-financing-options/) ). Converting the title is a required step, and the process depends on your state, so ask your lender and title company early.

### **Foundation choice is a financing choice.**


Common types include pier and beam, runner, slab, crawl space, and basement. The right one depends on your land, climate, local code, budget, and loan, and a lower-cost support system can narrow your loan options.


You can take a separate land loan and home loan, or a single land-home mortgage. Financing a factory-built home looks a lot like financing a site-built one. Your local[Cavco retailer](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-retailers) can point you to options in your area. Cavco has its own manufactured home financing company,[CountryPlace Mortgage](https://www.countryplaceloans.com/) .

## **What does site prep for a manufactured home involve?**


HUD’s installation standards (24 CFR Part 3285) set minimum rules for soil conditions, bearing capacity, drainage and ground moisture. The installation manual shipped with the home supplies the details, and states can set stricter rules.


Site prep then follows a set order:


1. **Clear.** Crews remove debris, sod and stumps from the footing area.


2. **Grade.** The lot is leveled, compacted and sloped so water runs away from the home. Federal rules call for a drop of at least half an inch per foot over the first ten feet. Poor grading can cause moisture problems and foundation movement.


3. **Build.** The foundation or support system and anchors go in.


4. **Connect.** Septic or sewer, water and electric service reach the site.


5. **Prepare access.** The driveway and delivery path get cleared and stabilized.


Walk the delivery route with the delivery team ahead of time. Check road width, tight turns, overhead lines and soft ground, since poor access can damage a home in transit.


Building permits may be needed for the foundation, porches, garages and utility work, sometimes as separate permits with separate fees. Installers must be licensed or approved through your state’s program or HUD’s, so confirm yours before you hire anyone.


## **Who handles site work, and what if you don’t own land yet?**


A[Cavco retailer](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-retailers) ‘s turnkey quote often includes the home, delivery, setting it on its foundation and basic site preparation. Septic, well, driveway and permits may vary by retailer. Ask which of those the quote covers and get a written list of who handles each one.


Buyers without land have options.[Cavco retailers](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-retailers) often help. Depending on the market, that can mean search tips, referrals to real estate professionals who know land for manufactured homes, retailer-owned lots, or move-in-ready homes already placed on land.


## **How much does site prep for a manufactured home cost?**


Costs swing with the lot and location. These figures from consumer sources give a rough idea of what you may spend, not actual estimates:


- **Perc test:** about $750 to $1,900 ([Angi](https://www.angi.com/articles/perc-test-cost.htm) , 2026)


- **Septic system:** $3,500 to $15,000 ([Angi](https://www.angi.com/articles/what-does-it-cost-install-septic-system.htm) , 2026)


- **Driveway:** $3,460 to $6,910 ([Fixr](https://www.fixr.com/costs/concrete-driveway-paving) , 2025)


Angi notes that most dealers include delivery and setup in the home price. Unimproved land, though, adds costs for permits, clearing, drainage and a driveway. Terrain, distance to utilities, soil results, flood-zone height and local fees all can change the total. Treat the ranges as starting points, not quotes. Ask for an itemized, written quote for all site work, and ask exactly what the home price includes.


## **How long does it take to prepare land for a manufactured home?**


No reliable national number exists, since timelines depend on the county and the lot. Soil evaluations and permits run on government schedules, so start them early. Foundation and site work can often go ahead as the home is being built, which is one reason factory-built homes often move faster than site-built ones.


## **Your next steps**


Make three calls this week: the planning office, the health department, and your lender. Use this checklist as you go.


### **Before you buy the land**


- Get zoning answers in writing


- Check the flood zone


- Confirm utilities, then schedule a soil evaluation


- Confirm legal access and order a survey


- Find the parcel’s HUD zones


### **Before you order the home**


- Ask your lender which loans and foundations fit


- Ask about title conversion


- Get a written scope of who handles what


- Request an itemized site-work quote


### **Before delivery**


- Finish clearing, grading, foundation, and utilities


- Confirm permits are issued


- Walk the delivery route


Then talk with your local[Cavco retailer](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-retailers) . Ready to see what’s available? Try the


[Find Your Home](https://www.cavcohomes.com/our-homes/us) tool to browse in-stock Cavco manufactured homes near you.


## **Land Prep FAQs**


### **Can you put a manufactured home on any piece of land?**


No. Zoning, utilities, legal access, flood rules, and lender requirements all apply to a manufactured home.


### **Does a manufactured home need a permanent foundation?**


For a mortgage that treats the home as real property, expect the lender to require one. Ask which type and whether an engineer's certification is needed.


### **Does a manufactured home need a septic system and a well?**


Outside city limits, usually yes, unless public sewer and water reach the lot.


### **When should you schedule a perc test?**


Before you close on the land. Some health departments use a different soil test, so ask which one your county requires.


### **Do you have to own the land to get a mortgage on a manufactured home?**


For FHA Title II loans, you usually must own the land or buy it with the home. Otherwise, a chattel loan is common. Ask your lender about options where you live.
